samples.question: The picture shows one cream board carrying a single thin slate-grey cord. The cord runs as a staircase of straight horizontal and vertical runs from one corner of the board to the opposite corner; it never crosses or touches itself, and one of its two ends is capped by a solid black disc. Twelve small coloured squares, the BEADS, sit on the cord. Each bead is red, orange, green, teal, blue or purple, and colours repeat. Every bead is either SOLID, filled right through with its colour, or HOLLOW, with a small cream window cut out of its middle. Solid and hollow beads have exactly the same outline, size and colour area apart from that window, so only the window tells them apart. Walk along the cord starting from the black capped end and read the beads in the order you meet them. In that order the beads form a properly nested bracket word: a solid bead OPENS a group, a hollow bead CLOSES the group that was opened most recently and is still open, and every group is opened and closed exactly once. The cord is not laid out simply left to right or top to bottom - it contains a run that doubles back - so the order along the cord is not the order of the beads by position, and sorting the beads by row, by column, or by straight-line distance from the black cap gives a different and wrong reading. Exactly one solid bead is surrounded by a magenta square frame. The bead that closes it is always at least five beads further along the cord, so it is never the next hollow bead you meet, and it is never the last bead on the cord. Bead colours are chosen independently of the bracket structure, and the answer colour is always worn by more than one bead, so no colour, position, size, count or amount of ink identifies the answer on its own. Find the hollow bead that closes the framed solid bead. What is the colour of that hollow bead? Answer red, orange, green, teal, blue or purple.
